title: The Yellow House on the Corner
description: The Yellow House on the Corner (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1980) is Rita Dove's first collection, published when she was twenty-seven. The Norton prints 'Geometry' from it, dated 1980, and the record covers the volume rather than the single poem because the anthology's selections are drawn from across its sections.
plot_or_argument: Dove's first book is unusually accomplished, and its distinguishing feature is the range of voices it takes on. The Akron poems are precise about place and class - a family in the industrial Midwest, a father's work, a house with a chimney - while 'This Life' lets Dove write in the first person of people she is not, from a nineteenth-century doctor to mythological women. 'Geometry' states the collection's aesthetic in miniature: the poem is interested in the forms that contain experience, in symmetry and the breaking of it, and in the moment when a pattern becomes visible. The book's title image, a yellow house on a corner, holds the two sides together, since a house is both a particular family's dwelling and a figure for the order the poems are making. Dove has said that the collection was written in the workshop years and that she was learning to use form to control feeling; what is striking on rereading is how little of it reads as apprentice work, and how much of her later manner - the sequence, the persona, the formal turn - is already present.
narrative_structure: Three sections of short lyrics and one sequence of persona poems; the volume moves from domestic and autobiographical poems to historical voices and back, and 'Geometry' is a single short lyric rather than a sequence.
meter_and_prosody: Metrically controlled free verse with frequent rhyme and near-rhyme; short lines and short poems; a diction that moves between the colloquial and the formal; and an image-based logic that prefers the shaped object to the statement.
historical_context: The book was published by Carnegie Mellon University Press in 1980, when Dove was teaching at Arizona State University after her Iowa MFA; it appeared in the same year as her second collection was in preparation, which is why the two are often discussed together. The late 1970s were the years in which a generation of Black poets born after the war - Dove, Komunyakaa, Yusef and others - began publishing first books that were neither Black Arts nor confessional.
literary_significance: The volume is Dove's debut and the source of the earliest poem the Norton prints; 'Geometry' is among the most anthologised of her short lyrics and is often used to introduce her formal control. The record is one of the two that answer the anthology's three Adolescence rows, since those poems come from the same period of her work.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Carnegie Mellon University Press (Pittsburgh) in 1980. The Norton prints 'Geometry' from it. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is family and the ordinary life of a Black family in Akron, treated without sociology. The second is the making of art out of that material, since 'Geometry' is a poem about form itself. The third is history, which enters through the persona poems. The fourth is childhood and the gaining of a self-consciousness that the poems both record and resist.
summary: The book is in three sections and moves between the domestic and the historical. Its poems include portraits of family members in Akron, poems about childhood and the body, and a sequence, 'This Life', in which Dove speaks in the voices of historical and mythological figures. 'Geometry' - the poem the Norton prints - is a short lyric about order, measurement and the shapes a life is fitted into, and it shows the formal preoccupations that run through the volume.
critical_context: Criticism treats the first book as the foundation of Dove's manner and notes that its persona poems anticipate Mother Love; the standard account of her development places the Akron poems and the 'This Life' sequence as the two poles between which her later work moves. 'Geometry' is usually discussed for its treatment of form as a subject.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the description rests on its table of contents and on the published accounts of Dove's early work. The first printing of the anthology's three Adolescence poems was not verified and is not asserted here.

title: Museum
description: Museum (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1983) is Rita Dove's second collection, and it is the one in which she began to write about Europe, art and the position of the observer. The Norton prints 'Parsley' and 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' from it.
plot_or_argument: Museum is Dove's argument with the museum as a way of seeing, and its two selections state both sides of the argument. 'Parsley' takes a historical atrocity and refuses to let it be contemplated from a distance: the poem moves between the general's voice, the soldiers' and the victims', and its repetitions of 'perejil' make the massacre happen in language rather than behind it. The poem's form - four numbered sections, a chorus of cane-cutters, a dictator's aria - is operatic, and its ambition is to do in lyric what a documentary cannot, which is to show how a word becomes an instrument of murder. 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' is the counterweight: a short, first-person refusal of the position of the museum visitor, of the aesthetic appreciation that turns suffering into an exhibit. Read together, the two poems define the book's subject as the ethics of looking, which is the same subject Dove would return to in the persona poems of Mother Love and in Sonata Mulattica.
narrative_structure: A collection of short lyrics and one long four-part narrative poem, arranged so that the museum poems and the history poems alternate; 'Parsley' is the volume's structural centre.
meter_and_prosody: Controlled free verse with rhyme and repetition; multiple voices inside a single poem; a plain, declarative line for the historical passages; and an imagery of paintings, mirrors and windows throughout.
historical_context: Museum appeared in 1983, the year before Dove began teaching at Arizona State, and it was written in part during and after her Fulbright year in Germany; its European poems come from that period, and 'Parsley' was researched from accounts of the 1937 massacre, in which Trujillo's soldiers killed an estimated 20,000 Haitians along the border. The poem's attention to the shibboleth of 'perejil' comes from the historical record.
literary_significance: 'Parsley' is Dove's most ambitious early poem and one of the most important American poems of the 1980s about state violence; it is a standard anthology piece and a Norton selection. With 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' it shows the anthology representing Dove's historical range as well as her domestic lyrics.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Carnegie Mellon University Press (Pittsburgh) in 1983. The Norton prints 'Parsley' and 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the museum and the gaze, and the book's title names the institution it is arguing with. The second is the history of racial violence, above all in 'Parsley'. The third is the artist's relation to European culture, which Dove approaches as a Black American visitor rather than as an heir. The fourth is the refusal of contemplation, which is an aesthetic as well as a moral position.
summary: The collection moves between poems written out of travel in Europe - museums, paintings, cathedrals, the Mediterranean - and poems about American history and the body, and its central poem is 'Parsley', a long narrative lyric about the 1937 massacre of Haitian cane-cutters in the Dominican Republic on the orders of Rafael Trujillo. That poem's device is the dictator's inability to pronounce the Spanish word for parsley, 'perejil', which was used to identify Haitians by their accent, and Dove builds a four-part poem around the word and the killing. 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' is a short lyric about refusing the aesthetic distance that museums teach.
critical_context: Criticism reads 'Parsley' as a landmark of the American historical lyric and discusses its operatic structure and its use of the shibboleth; the ethics of Dove's multiple voicing - whether a non-Haitian poet can speak the victims' chorus - has been debated. Museum as a whole is usually treated as the book in which Dove's interest in art and history became explicit.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the description of 'Parsley' rests on its published text and the poem's standard critical accounts, and the casualty figure is given as the historical estimates give it, not as the poem states it.

title: Thomas and Beulah
description: Thomas and Beulah (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1986) won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1987. It is a book-length sequence in two halves, telling the lives of Dove's maternal grandparents - Thomas, who came north from Tennessee to work in Akron, and Beulah, who married him - and the Norton prints three of its poems: 'The Event', 'The Zeppelin Factory' and 'Dusting'.
plot_or_argument: The book's achievement is to give two ordinary lives the scale of history without inflating them. Dove works in short lyrics arranged in sequence, and the sequence does the work that prose would do: the reader assembles a marriage out of moments, and the gaps between poems are as significant as the poems. Thomas's half is full of the world - the Great Migration, the war, the zeppelin works, the race riot of 1919 in Akron and the labour organising of the 1930s - while Beulah's half is full of the house, and the asymmetry is the book's argument about the different freedoms of men and women in the same life. The poems are in the third person and refuse the poet's commentary; Dove does not tell the reader what her grandparents' lives mean, and the sequence's last poems, in which Beulah is dying among her daughters, are remarkable for their calm. The title's two names give the book its form: it is a double portrait, and the two halves are not equal in the amount of the world they can reach. The Pulitzer made Dove, at thirty-four, the second African American poet to win it, and the book has become the standard model for the American book-length family sequence. Its most important technical decision is that neither half narrates its own meaning: the reader is given the objects - a mandolin, a lemon tree, a zeppelin, a dust cloth - and left to assemble the lives from them, which is why the sequence rewards reading in order rather than in excerpts.
narrative_structure: Two halves of about twenty-five short poems each, in chronological order within each half, with the two lives running in parallel rather than interleaved; the poems are short lyrics, many of a single stanza, and no poem comments on another.
meter_and_prosody: Third-person lyrics in controlled free verse with rhyme; plain diction and domestic objects; the historical world admitted through names, machines and dates rather than through statement; and an absence of the poet's 'I'.
historical_context: The book appeared in 1986 from Carnegie Mellon and won the Pulitzer in 1987, the year of Toni Morrison's Beloved and of a wider public argument about African American family history; Dove's grandparents had migrated from Tennessee to Akron, and the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company, where Thomas worked and where Dove's father became the company's first Black chemist, is the book's industrial ground.
literary_significance: Thomas and Beulah is one of the most honoured American poetry books of the 1980s and is the work for which Dove is best known; its model of the documentary family sequence has been widely imitated, and the Norton's three selections from it give the anthology the book's scale as well as its individual lyrics. With the three Adolescence poems and four other lyrics, Dove has ten selections in the period, more than any other poet.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Carnegie Mellon University Press (Pittsburgh) in 1986; Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, 1987. The Norton prints 'The Event', 'The Zeppelin Factory' and 'Dusting'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Great Migration, since Thomas's journey north is the book's historical engine. The second is marriage and its asymmetry, which the two-part structure embodies. The third is labour, both industrial and domestic, and the way it shapes a body. The fourth is memory and inheritance, since the poet is reconstructing lives she knows only through family story.
summary: The first half, 'Mandolin', follows Thomas from his arrival in Akron and the death of his friend Lem, through courtship, marriage, the birth of four daughters and his work at the Goodyear factory, to the lemons he grows in old age. The second half, 'Canary in Bloom', follows Beulah from her marriage through the household, her illness, her widowhood and her death. 'The Event' is one of the poems of Thomas's early life, 'The Zeppelin Factory' recalls the airship works in Akron and the men who worked in it, and 'Dusting' is a short poem of Beulah's domestic life.
critical_context: Criticism reads the sequence as a recovery of Black family history in the Great Migration and discusses its refusal of the poet's voice, its use of the two-part structure to mark gender difference, and its handling of the 1919 Akron riot and the zeppelin works. The Pulitzer is usually treated as the moment Dove became a public poet, and the book as the model for the documentary sequences of the 1990s.
research_notes: The sequence was not read in full for this record; the description rests on its published structure and on the standard critical accounts, and the placement of the three printed poems in their halves is given from the sequence's contents. Internal dates such as the 1919 Akron riot are given as the historical record, not as the poems' own statements.

title: The Business of Fancydancing
description: The Business of Fancydancing: Stories and Poems (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1992) is Sherman Alexie's first book, published when he was twenty-five. It mixes short stories and poems without marking the boundary, and the Norton prints 'Pawn Shop' from it.
plot_or_argument: The book's formal oddity is its refusal to separate poetry from prose, and that refusal is its argument: on the reservation, a story and a poem are the same act, and the distinction belongs to the publisher. Alexie's early voice is direct, funny and wounded, and it uses the materials of late-twentieth-century American popular culture - basketball, television, beer, cars - as if they were a literary inheritance, which for his characters they are. 'Pawn Shop' shows the method in miniature: a flat, reportorial prose that lists what is being exchanged and what it costs, and a refusal to explain the transaction's meaning. The book's politics are inseparable from its comedy, since the jokes are about the conditions the poems are also mourning, and the title's irony - that Indian identity is a business - is the collection's central insight. Its publication by Hanging Loose, a small Brooklyn press, placed Alexie outside the university and the Native American studies circuit, and its success made him the most visible Native writer of his generation while he was still in his twenties.
narrative_structure: A collection of short lyrics, prose poems and short stories in roughly chronological arrangement by the age of the speaker, with no section headings separating the genres.
literary_form: Collection of poems and short stories (debut volume)
meter_and_prosody: Short lines and very short paragraphs; a demotic, joke-timed voice; brand names and basketball as common reference; repetition and a deliberate flatness at moments of grief; and no figurative heightening.
historical_context: Hanging Loose Press published the book in 1992, the year Alexie graduated from Washington State University, and it appeared in the same season as The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven (1993), which followed within a year. The early 1990s were the years of the Native American literary boom created by the successes of Momaday, Silko, Erdrich and Welch, and Alexie's debut was read as the arrival of an urban, pop-culture Indian voice.
literary_significance: The book is the debut of the most widely read Native American writer of his generation and the source of one of the Norton's four Alexie selections; it establishes the mixed-genre form he would keep, and 'Pawn Shop' is a standard example of his prose poem. The Norton list carried 'Pawn Shop' as undated before this wave; this record fixes it at 1992.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Hanging Loose Press (Brooklyn) in 1992. The Norton prints 'Pawn Shop'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is reservation life and its economies, both the pawn shop and the powwow. The second is alcoholism and loss, which the book treats without moralising. The third is the performance of Indianness for white expectations, which the title names. The fourth is family and the inheritance of damage, carried in the book's short, unexplained scenes.
summary: The book's seventy-odd pieces are set on and around the Spokane reservation and move between first-person lyrics, prose poems and very short stories. Its subjects are drinking, basketball, family violence, the deaths of friends and the business of being an Indian in front of white readers - the title's 'fancydancing' is both the powwow dance and the performance of identity for an audience. 'Pawn Shop' is one of its prose pieces, a single-paragraph narrative about the commerce of the reservation town.
critical_context: Criticism reads the debut as a departure from the ceremonial mode of the Native American Renaissance, noting its demotic voice and its refusal of anthropological explanation; the standard account of Alexie's career treats the first book as the source of the tone he developed in the stories and films.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the description rests on its published contents and on the standard accounts of Alexie's early work. The 1992 date fixes the Norton list's undated row.

title: The Summer of Black Widows
description: The Summer of Black Widows (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1996) is Sherman Alexie's second collection of poems, published in the year of his novel Indian Killer. The Norton prints 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' from its third sequence, a group of poems about the death of his sister in a house fire.
plot_or_argument: The collection shows Alexie working in received forms - the villanelle, the sestina - while keeping his demotic voice, and 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' is the clearest example: a villanelle's two refrains are made to do the work of grief, so that the form's repetition becomes the obsessive return of the mourner. The sequence it closes moves from the fire itself through the family's aftermath to the brother's guilt at having survived and at having made art from the death, and the last poem's formal control is the point - the discipline is what the grief is being held in. Alexie's habit of undercutting solemnity with a joke is present even here, which makes the poem harder rather than easier. The collection as a whole is more various than the debut: it includes love poems, a long poem about basketball and a sequence on the Spokane world, and its range is what the Norton's selection represents, a poet who can write a villanelle about his sister and a joke about Crazy Horse in the same book.
narrative_structure: A collection of sequences, with the sister poems forming the third and the villanelle placed last in it; the poems are short and the sequences are held together by recurring images rather than narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Demotic free verse with formal poems set among it; a villanelle with two refrains; jokes inside elegies; and a line that is closer to speech than to song.
historical_context: The collection appeared in 1996, the year of Indian Killer, and belongs to the period in which Alexie was publishing a book a year; Hanging Loose had published his debut and remained his publisher for poetry. His sister's death in a house fire is the biographical ground of the sequence, and the poems are unusual among his work for their directness about family loss.
literary_significance: The collection contains Alexie's most formally accomplished poem and is the source of the Norton's third poem selection; 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' is regularly cited in discussions of the villanelle in contemporary American poetry, which is a surprising place to find a Spokane writer and exactly the point. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave; this record fixes it at 1996.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Hanging Loose Press (Brooklyn) in 1996. The Norton prints 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the death of a sibling and the guilt of the survivor, which the sequence treats without consolation. The second is the relation of art to grief, since the brother is a writer and the poem knows it. The third is family and the reservation world in which the loss happens. The fourth is the book's own arrangement, since the sequences are ordered so that the poems of courtship and the poems of the fire sit in the same volume without either explaining the other.
summary: The book is in several sequences and mixes love poems, political poems, poems about basketball and a long central sequence about the death of Alexie's sister. 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' is a villanelle, the last poem of that sequence, in which the brother mourns the sister and confronts his own survival; the poem's repeated lines carry both the fire and the smoke that is left of the person.
critical_context: Criticism notes Alexie's use of received forms as a claim on the tradition and discusses the sister sequence as his most direct treatment of grief; the standard account of the collection reads it as the book in which he proved he was a poet as well as a storyteller.
research_notes: The collection's date is confirmed from its publication record; the individual poems' first periodical appearances were not traced. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave.

title: At Navajo Monument Valley Tribal School
description: 'At Navajo Monument Valley Tribal School' is a poem from The Business of Fancydancing (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1992), Alexie's first book. It is about a photograph of students at an Indian boarding school, and it is the most directly historical poem in his debut.
plot_or_argument: The poem's method is ekphrasis as indictment: the photograph is treated as a document and as a lie at the same time, since the order and cleanliness of the line-up are exactly what the school was for. Alexie's short lines let him place a fact beside an image without arguing, and the poem's power comes from the reader's knowledge of what the boarding schools did - the cutting of hair, the prohibition of Native languages, the separation of children from parents, the motto 'kill the Indian, save the man'. The poem does not supply that history, and its refusal to explain is a refusal to make the children into a lesson. It is also one of the earliest poems in which Alexie writes about photography, a subject he returns to throughout his work, and its treatment of the camera as an instrument of both record and violence is characteristic of the Native American writing of the period, which had begun to read the photographic archive against itself.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem in brief lines, organised as a reading of a single photograph with no stanza division and no narrative development.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; present tense; a flat descriptive tone that refuses outrage; and an absence of simile, so that the photograph stays a photograph.
historical_context: The Business of Fancydancing appeared in 1992, and the poem belongs to the period of public reckoning with the boarding-school system that would produce the 2000s scholarship on it; Navajo Monument Valley Tribal School is a school on the Navajo Nation, and the poem's title names a specific institution rather than a generic one.
literary_significance: The poem is the historical centre of Alexie's debut and the one most often taught in courses on boarding-school literature; it is a Norton selection, and the list carried it as undated before this wave.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Business of Fancydancing (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1992). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Indian boarding school and the assimilation policy it served. The second is the photograph as a document that records and conceals at once. The third is the survival of the children in the picture, which the poem insists on without sentiment. The fourth is language, since the schools' central act was to forbid it.
summary: The poem describes a photograph of Navajo children lined up at a tribal school, and it reads the image for what it does not show: the children's names, the languages they were forbidden, the families they were taken from. It moves between the photograph's flat surface and the history the surface holds down, and its short lines keep the poem close to the picture rather than letting it escape into statement.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem with the photographic archive of the boarding schools and treats its refusal to narrate as its ethical choice; the standard account of Alexie's early work places it among the poems that carry the book's historical weight.
research_notes: The collection's date is confirmed from its publication record; the poem's first periodical appearance was not traced. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave.

title: The Joy Luck Club
description: The Joy Luck Club (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1989) is Amy Tan's first novel: sixteen interlinked stories in which four Chinese immigrant mothers and their four American-born daughters each narrate in the first person. The Norton prints 'Two Kinds', the chapter in which Jing-mei Woo recalls her mother's attempt to make her a child prodigy.
plot_or_argument: The novel's form is its argument. By giving each of eight women two chapters, Tan refuses the single generational narrative in which the immigrant mother is the past and the American daughter the future; instead the mothers' Chinese lives are rendered with the same novelistic weight as the daughters' American ones, and the reader learns the mothers' stories before the daughters do. Tan's prose is deliberately plain and her chapters are built as anecdote and testimony rather than plot, which lets the book keep the cadence of the dinner table and the mahjong table. 'Two Kinds' is the book's most anthologised chapter because it dramatises the whole relation in a single childhood: the mother's belief that America means a daughter can be anything, the daughter's refusal to be anything in particular, and the piano - a broken-down instrument that Jing-mei is given and that she plays badly - as the object through which the two of them communicate their love and their wounds. The chapter's famous last line, that the two songs they played were 'two halves of the same song', states the novel's whole thesis in a domestic image. Tan's refusal of the reunion plot is part of the design: the daughters do not learn their mothers' stories in the order the book tells them, and the reader's knowledge runs ahead of theirs, which makes the act of reading itself an image of inheritance.
narrative_structure: Four sections of four chapters, each opening with a short mother's parable; eight first-person narrators alternate, with mothers and daughters paired; the stories move backwards into China and forwards into California rather than chronologically.
meter_and_prosody: Plain first-person prose in eight distinguishable voices; Chinese words and sayings left untranslated in the mothers' speech; short chapters built as anecdote; and a syntax that keeps the rhythm of oral narration.
historical_context: The novel appeared in 1989 and spent months on the New York Times bestseller list; it was filmed by Wayne Wang in 1993 with a screenplay Tan co-wrote. Its publication belongs to the years in which Asian American literature entered the mainstream - Maxine Hong Kingston's The Woman Warrior had appeared in 1976 - and its reception was also the occasion for a debate about the authenticity of the Chinese material, which Tan answered in The Opposite of Fate.
literary_significance: The Joy Luck Club is the most commercially successful novel by an Asian American writer and the book that made the Chinese American immigrant family a mainstream literary subject; 'Two Kinds' is a standard anthology text in courses on the immigrant bildungsroman and on mother-daughter writing. The Norton's printing of it places Tan beside Kingston in the anthology's representation of Asian American prose.
bibliographical_notes: First published by G. P. Putnam's Sons (New York) in 1989. The Norton prints the chapter 'Two Kinds'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the gulf between the mothers' Chinese past and the daughters' American present, which the structure makes a matter of information rather than judgement. The second is the model-minority pressure, since the mothers' ambitions for their daughters carry both hope and the history of what they lost. The third is migration and the untold family story, since the mothers' losses in China are the book's buried substance. The fourth is the act of storytelling itself, which the novel presents as the only inheritance that survives the crossing.
summary: The book is framed by a mahjong game. Suyuan Woo has died, and her daughter Jing-mei is asked to take her place at the Joy Luck Club, the four-family investment and mahjong group Suyuan founded in San Francisco; the mothers were all born in China and came to America after the war, and the daughters were raised in California. Each of the four sections of the book carries a short parable from a mother and two longer stories, one by a mother and one by a daughter, and the stories run back into the 1920s, the Japanese invasion, the war and the loss of children. 'Two Kinds' is Jing-mei's account of being nine and drilled by her mother in arithmetic, memory tests and piano, of the disastrous recital at a talent show, and of the quarrel in which she tells her mother she wishes she had never been born and her mother replies that there are two kinds of daughters, those who obey and those who do not.
critical_context: Criticism reads the book through the mahjong structure and the mother-daughter pairs, and debates whether Tan's Chinese sections constitute historical recovery or exotic backdrop; the standard account treats the narrative design as the novel's main achievement. 'Two Kinds' is regularly discussed for its handling of the mother's ambition as an inheritance of loss rather than as tyranny.
research_notes: The novel was not read in full for this record; 'Two Kinds' was read in its published form and the rest of the description rests on the book's structure and the standard critical accounts. The chapter's page range in the anthology was not established.

title: Woman Hollering Creek
description: 'Woman Hollering Creek' is the title story of Sandra Cisneros's second collection, Woman Hollering Creek and Other Stories (New York: Random House, 1991). It is about a Mexican woman brought to Texas as a bride, and it takes its title from a creek near San Antonio and from the legend of La Llorona, the weeping woman.
plot_or_argument: The story is a rewriting of La Llorona, and its whole point is to refuse the legend's verdict. In the folktale the woman who loses her children to water weeps for them forever, and the crying is a punishment; Cisneros takes the creek's name and asks who is hollering and why, and gives the answer to a woman driver who shouts for the pleasure of it. Cleófilas's education in what a woman's life can be comes from two sources, both of them popular: the telenovelas, which teach her that passion means suffering, and Felice, whose truck and laughter teach her the opposite. The story's style is clipped and repetitive, with short sentences and a refrain-like return to the creek, and the Spanish is left untranslated so that the reader who does not know it is placed where Cleófilas is when she crosses the border. Its ending is deliberately not a resolution: Cleófilas is being driven somewhere, and the story stops at the moment of possibility rather than the arrival, which is what has made it a standard text in courses on domestic violence and narrative ethics. The story's Spanish is left in the text for the same reason: a reader who does not know the language is placed where Cleófilas stands when she crosses the border, hearing a country she cannot yet answer in.
narrative_structure: A short story in short sections that move between Cleófilas's interiority and a reportorial outside view, with a refrain-like return to the creek and an open ending in a moving truck.
literary_form: Short story (title story of the collection)
meter_and_prosody: Short declarative sentences with heavy repetition; Spanish and English mixed without glossing; a third person that moves close to and away from Cleófilas; and a flat, almost deadpan tone at moments of violence.
historical_context: The collection appeared in 1991, seven years after The House on Mango Street, and its stories move between Mexico and Texas; the story's geography is the real Woman Hollering Creek near San Antonio, and its legal background is the domestic-violence shelter movement of the 1980s. Cisneros has said the story came from hearing the creek's name and wanting to know who hollered.
literary_significance: 'Woman Hollering Creek' is the most anthologised Chicana short story after Cisneros's own 'Barbie-Q' and is a standard text for the study of domestic violence in literature; it is the story through which the Norton represents Cisneros, and with Anzaldúa's essays it gives the anthology the Chicana presence of the 1980s and 1990s.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Woman Hollering Creek and Other Stories (New York: Random House, 1991). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is domestic violence and the isolation that makes it possible, rendered without any explanatory apparatus. The second is the border as a place where women's lives are exchanged between families. The third is the folklore of the weeping woman, which the story rewrites as a figure of freedom. The fourth is the popular culture of the telenovela, treated as a real teacher of desire and of its limits.
summary: Cleófilas is a young woman from a small town in Mexico who marries Juan Pedro and comes to live in Seguín, Texas, near the creek the Texans call Woman Hollering Creek. Her life becomes the telenovelas she watched at home: a husband who drinks, beats her and leaves her alone with a baby, and a house at the edge of a highway. She writes to her father and does not tell him. When she becomes pregnant again and is beaten, a neighbour takes her to a clinic in San Antonio and a woman called Felice drives her away in a pickup truck, and the story ends with Cleófilas's surprise at Felice's laughter, her hollering, her freedom.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story's rewriting of La Llorona as its central act and discusses the ending's refusal of closure as an ethical choice; the story's use of untranslated Spanish has been much discussed as a way of positioning the reader inside the border experience. It is regularly taught with Anzaldúa's 'How to Tame a Wild Tongue'.
research_notes: The story was read for this record from its published text; the first periodical appearance, if any, was not established, and the collection's 1991 imprint is the date given.

title: Fleur
description: 'Fleur' is a chapter of Louise Erdrich's Love Medicine (New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1984), published separately as a story before the novel appeared and printed by the Norton as a selection in its own right. It is set in 1913 and tells of Fleur Pillager, the woman at the centre of Erdrich's fictional world.
plot_or_argument: 'Fleur' is Erdrich's most concentrated treatment of the figure who organises her whole fiction, and its method is to make the supernatural inseparable from the realistic. Fleur's power is never explained and never doubted: the men who assault her are destroyed by a storm that arrives at the exact moment, and the story's tone - Pauline's schoolgirlish, spiteful, fascinated narration - never explains the connection, so that the reader is left inside a world where the two orders are continuous. Pauline's unreliability is the story's engine: she is jealous of Fleur, ashamed of her own Chippewa blood, and increasingly drawn to Catholic martyrdom, and her account is shaped by what she cannot admit about herself. The story's treatment of sexual violence is remarkable for the period in refusing both victimhood and revenge: Fleur is not saved by a man and does not need to be, and her departure is the story's only judgement. The prose is plain and the dialogue idiomatic, with the butcher shop and the meat locker rendered in exact sensory detail against the lake's mythic presence. Erdrich's decision to give the story to Pauline rather than to Fleur is the whole design: the reader never enters Fleur's mind, and so her power remains as unaccountable to us as it is to the butcher shop, which is exactly how the Chippewa world is presented in the novels that grew from this chapter.
narrative_structure: A first-person retrospective narration by Pauline Puyat, in a sequence of scenes that move from Fleur's arrival to her departure, with a storm as the climax and no explanation offered for it.
literary_form: Chapter of Love Medicine (published as a short story and as a chapter)
meter_and_prosody: Plain, idiomatic first-person prose in a period voice; a narrator whose judgements are visible and unreliable; concrete detail of work, meat, cards and weather; and a refusal to allegorise the supernatural.
historical_context: Love Medicine was published in 1984 and expanded in 1993; 'Fleur' appeared as a story first, in the 1980s, and was incorporated into the novel's earlier chapters. Its 1913 setting places it before the novel's main action and makes it the origin story of the Pillager line; the reservation land, allotment and the loss of the Pillager woods are the historical ground of the whole sequence of novels that followed.
literary_significance: 'Fleur' is the story through which Erdrich's mythic method is usually introduced and the chapter on which the reading of Love Medicine as a Native American novel of the supernatural most often rests; it is a standard anthology text and a Norton selection. Its publication as a story before the novel is a useful case of the way Erdrich's books were assembled from separately published pieces.
bibliographical_notes: Published as a story before its appearance as a chapter of Love Medicine (New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1984); the expanded edition of the novel followed in 1993. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is Fleur herself - a woman of power whose power is not explained in the story's Christian or legal terms. The second is sexual violence and the community's response to it. The third is the relation of the Chippewa world to the white town, which the story figures in the lake, the woods and the butcher shop. The fourth is Pauline's own self-hatred and religious mania, which is the story's psychological subject.
summary: The story is narrated by Pauline Puyat, a mixed-blood girl who works in the butcher shop in Argus, North Dakota, and who watches Fleur Pillager arrive in town with a reputation. Fleur is a Chippewa woman who has already survived being drowned in Lake Matchimanito and who is said to have taken the life of a man in a card game; she works at the butcher shop, takes the men's money at cards, and is assaulted by three men in the meat locker, after which a tornado destroys the butcher shop and the men are ruined. The story ends with Fleur walking away from the town and Pauline following her.
critical_context: Criticism reads 'Fleur' for its handling of narrative unreliability, for the continuity of the supernatural and the real, and for its treatment of sexual violence; the standard account of Love Medicine treats the chapter as the first appearance of the figure who links the novels. Pauline Puyat's narration is regularly discussed as one of Erdrich's most complex voices.
research_notes: The story was read in its published form. The exact place and date of its first separate publication were not established for this record, and the date given is that of Love Medicine's first edition; the anthology's own page reference was not checked.

title: The Gift
description: 'The Gift' is in Rose (Rochester: BOA Editions, 1986), Li-Young Lee's first collection. It is a short narrative poem in which a father removes a splinter from his son's hand and the son remembers his own father doing the same for him.
plot_or_argument: The poem's subject is inheritance as a technique of tenderness, and its structure is a single gesture repeated across two generations. Lee does not name the father's history of exile or imprisonment, and that omission is what makes the poem work: the tenderness is inherited without explanation, and the reader who knows the biography fills in what the father's talking was for. The poem's plainness is deliberate - short unpunctuated lines, no figurative heightening, no emotional vocabulary - and the whole weight of the poem is carried by the two hands and the knife. 'The Gift' is one of the most widely taught poems in contemporary American poetry precisely because it does so much with so little: it is a poem about a small kindness that turns out to be a legacy, and 1986's other Lee poems in the anthology - which deal with hunger, memory and the father's death - are the context in which this quiet poem does its work.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse narrative in short lines, built on the repetition of the same action in two times, with no stanza divisions and an ending on the image of the hands.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; a plain, declarative syntax; almost no adjectives of feeling; the father's speech quoted directly and left banal; and a refusal of simile.
historical_context: Rose appeared from BOA Editions in 1986 and won the Delmore Schwartz Memorial Award; its poems draw on Lee's childhood in Indonesia, the family's flight and his father's ministry in Pennsylvania. The collection belongs to the wave of Asian American poetry that followed Cathy Song's Picture Bride and Marilyn Chin's work in the early 1980s, and BOA was the small press through which several of Lee's generation reached readers.
literary_significance: 'The Gift' is the most anthologised poem in Rose and one of the most widely taught American poems of the 1980s; it is a Norton selection and the poem through which Lee is represented in most courses. Its craft - the small scene, the inherited gesture - is standard material in courses on the narrative lyric.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Rose (Rochester, NY: BOA Editions, 1986). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the father-son relation as inheritance, and specifically the inheritance of a way of acting rather than a belief. The second is memory, since the speaker's present act releases the remembered one. The third is care as a physical skill, which the poem treats as an art. The fourth is the unspoken history of the family, present in the poem only as the father's talking.
summary: The poem's present-tense scene is a father taking a metal splinter out of his son's palm with a knife, and the father's method is to talk - about the weather, about the neighbours - so that the boy will not look. The son, now a man, remembers that his own father did the same for him, with the same talk, and the poem holds the two scenes together so that the speaker's hands are both the boy's and the father's. The tone is quiet and the poem finishes with the sense that the gift is not the removal of the splinter but the manner of it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an example of the contemporary narrative lyric and discusses its refusal of the father's history; the standard account of Lee's early work treats 'The Gift' with 'Persimmons' as the two poems that established his manner.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from the collection; a first periodical appearance, if any, was not established.

title: Persimmons
description: 'Persimmons' is in Rose (Rochester: BOA Editions, 1986), Li-Young Lee's first collection. It is his most famous poem, and it turns on a single word - persimmon - that the speaker learns wrongly in school and then reclaims from his father.
plot_or_argument: The poem's subject is the recovery of a language that was taken away, and its method is sensory repetition: the persimmon is described by its skin, its flesh and its taste, and the vocabulary that the teacher's slap had punished becomes the poem's incantation. Lee's handling of the father's blindness is the poem's emotional centre - the hands that read the fruit are the same hands that once wrote and are now the speaker's inheritance - and the poem refuses both pathos and politics. Its final movement, in which the father asks to be buried with persimmons so that he can eat them in the afterlife, is funny and devastating at once, and the shift of register is one of the things the poem is admired for. The poem's structure is associative: each memory produces the next, and the word 'persimmon' returns as a refrain that holds the poem together, so that the language the speaker lost at school becomes the form of the poem itself.
narrative_structure: A free-verse lyric in short sections that move by association between school, childhood, father and wife, with the word 'persimmon' repeated as a refrain.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines; sensory and tactile imagery; a plain declarative syntax interrupted by direct speech; and a repeated single word used as an incantation.
historical_context: Rose appeared in 1986; 'Persimmons' is its most discussed poem and is regularly taught as a founding text of Asian American poetics, since it turns the immigrant child's linguistic punishment into an ars poetica. The poem's persimmon is the Japanese and Chinese fruit, and the ripening trick with an apple is a household method rather than a literary allusion.
literary_significance: 'Persimmons' is one of the most widely anthologised Asian American poems and a standard text in courses on language and identity; with 'The Gift' and 'Eating Together' it gives the Norton three of the five Lee poems it prints, and its use of an untranslatable word as refrain is regularly cited as a model for the poetry of the diaspora.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Rose (Rochester, NY: BOA Editions, 1986). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is language and the shame of not having the right words, which the school scene establishes. The second is the father's blindness, treated as a way of knowing rather than a lack. The third is food and the body, since the poem's knowledge arrives through taste and touch. The fourth is the recovery of a Chinese past in English, which is the whole larger subject of Lee's generation of Asian American poets.
summary: The poem begins with the speaker as a schoolboy who is slapped by a teacher for failing to distinguish 'persimmon' from 'precision' in a spelling test, and it moves through his memories of his blind father and the fruit. It describes the father's hands feeling the persimmons to know whether they are ripe, the mother's method of ripening them in a bowl with an apple, and the speaker's own learning of the fruit's forms - the skin, the flesh, the blossom - in a sequence of tactile images. It ends with the speaker's love-making compared to the fruit and with his father's blindness and death, and the word 'persimmon' recurs as a chant.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a drama of language acquisition and loss, and discusses the father's blindness as a vehicle of cultural memory; the standard account treats the poem's refrain and its associative structure as its formal achievement. It is one of the few poems of the period that is taught at both secondary and graduate level.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from the collection; a first periodical appearance, if any, was not established.

title: Eating Alone
description: 'Eating Alone' is in Rose (Rochester: BOA Editions, 1986), Li-Young Lee's first collection. It is an elegy for the poet's father, spoken while the son eats alone in the garden the father planted.
plot_or_argument: The poem's method is to keep the elegy inside the senses, so that grief arrives as vegetables rather than as statement. Lee's father was a physician and a minister who had been imprisoned and exiled before coming to America, and the garden he planted in Pennsylvania is the poem's ground - unlike the earlier 'The Gift', where the father passes on a technique of touch, 'Eating Alone' inherits a plot of ground and the labour invested in it. The poem's short unpunctuated lines move by association from one vegetable to another, and its syntax has the flatness of a man talking to himself at a table, which is exactly what the poem is. Its refusal to console is what distinguishes it: the father is not in the garden in any metaphysical sense, the garden is simply where his work remains, and the poem finds that sufficient. That ordinary consolation - the meal, the soil, the light - is what Lee's early poems consistently offer instead of the transcendent, and it is why they are read as poems of the household rather than of the afterlife.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse poem in short lines, moving from the garden's produce to the father's absence and back to the present meal, with no formal climax.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; exact horticultural and culinary detail; a conversational syntax with direct address; and no figurative heightening at the line of grief.
historical_context: Rose appeared in 1986 and its poems about the father were written after his death in 1984; the family's garden in Pennsylvania is the setting of several of them. The collection belongs to the first wave of Asian American poetry published by small presses in the 1980s, and BOA Editions was its publisher.
literary_significance: The poem is one of the most frequently anthologised poems in Rose and a standard elegy in courses on contemporary American poetry; it is a Norton selection, and with 'The Gift' it shows the two kinds of inheritance - an act of care and a piece of ground - that Lee's first book is built from.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Rose (Rochester, NY: BOA Editions, 1986). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is mourning and the continuing presence of the dead in what they made. The second is food and agriculture as the form that love takes between generations. The third is solitude, which the poem treats without self-pity. The fourth is the garden as a living inheritance, which is the poem's answer to loss.
summary: The speaker is eating alone in a garden of vegetables and remembers that his father planted them; he describes the light, the rows of onions and spinach, the smell of the earth, and the fact that the father who made the garden is dead. The poem moves between the physical present - food, soil, sun - and the absent man, and it ends with the speaker's recognition that the garden is a form of company and that the father's labour continues in it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem with the other paternal elegies of Rose and treats its refusal of consolation as characteristic of Lee's early manner; the standard account of the collection notes that its garden poems and its exile poems are the same poems seen from different sides.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from the collection; a first periodical appearance, if any, was not established.

title: Eating Together
description: 'Eating Together' is in Rose (Rochester: BOA Editions, 1986). It is a short lyric of a family at a meal in the years of the father's illness, and it is the companion poem to 'Eating Alone'.
plot_or_argument: 'Eating Together' is a poem about the ordinary as the only available consolation, and its technique is the unemphasised juxtaposition of the meal and the death. Lee does not announce the father's condition; he describes the food and lets the reader understand from the details - the father's thinness, the care with which he is served - that this is a last supper in the household rather than a feast. The poem's short lines and its plain diction keep it from becoming sentimental, and its close, in which the father's spoon is mentioned beside the son's hunger, is a model of how to end a poem on an object rather than a statement. Together with 'Eating Alone' it shows Lee's method across a collection: the same table, the same food, first with the father present and then without him, so that the two poems read as a single elegy in two parts.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse lyric in brief lines, organised as a single meal and ending on an object rather than a statement.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; domestic and culinary detail; a quiet, even tone; and an absence of metaphor, so that the spoon and the plate carry the poem's weight.
historical_context: Rose appeared in 1986, two years after the death of Lee's father; the poem's illness and its meal belong to that period, and its setting is the family's house in Pennsylvania. The collection's poems of the table are among the earliest in American poetry to treat the Asian immigrant household as a subject of lyric rather than of sociology.
literary_significance: The poem is a standard selection from Rose and is regularly taught alongside 'Eating Alone' and 'The Gift' as a sequence on family and food; it is a Norton selection and part of the anthology's unusually full representation of a single collection.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Rose (Rochester, NY: BOA Editions, 1986). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the family meal as the place where love is enacted and loss anticipated. The second is the father's illness, present in the poem's details rather than its statements. The third is the intimacy of a marriage, since the wife is at the table and the poem is partly addressed to her. The fourth is the immigrant household, where the food carries a homeland the family no longer lives in.
summary: The poem describes a family at the table - the speaker, his wife Donna, his mother, and his father in his last illness - and the food they are eating. It holds the ordinary detail of the meal against the knowledge that the father is dying, and its last movement places the father's spoon and the son's hunger in the same sentence. The tone is quiet and the poem finds in the meal a form of tenderness that none of the family can say.
critical_context: Criticism pairs the poem with 'Eating Alone' as the two halves of Lee's elegy for his father and reads its closing object as characteristic of his refusal of statement; the standard account of Rose treats the table poems as the book's centre.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from the collection; a first periodical appearance, if any, was not established.

title: I Ask My Mother to Sing
description: 'I Ask My Mother to Sing' is in Rose (Rochester: BOA Editions, 1986). It is a short poem in which the speaker asks his mother to sing a song about a lake in China, and the song brings back a country neither of them has seen in the same way.
plot_or_argument: The poem is about music as the last vehicle of a lost place, and its technique is to let the song take over the room. Lee does not describe the mother's feelings directly; he describes the song's images, and as the song proceeds those images become the poem's own setting, so that the reader is taken into the lake along with the family. The mother's singing and the father's joining are acts of memory that do not require the exiles to say what they have lost, and the poem's tenderness lies in the son's asking - the poem's title is an act of care as much as a request for a song. It is one of the most straightforwardly moving poems in Rose and one of the least complicated in its means: a room, two voices, a song and a lake.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse lyric of short lines, moving from the request to the song's images and ending inside the song's landscape.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; repetition of the song's imagery; a simple narrative syntax; and a closing movement that abandons the room for the imagined lake.
historical_context: Rose appeared in 1986; the poem belongs to the sequence of poems about Lee's parents and their lost China, which run through the collection alongside the father elegies. The song the mother sings is a Chinese popular song, and the poem leaves its words untranslated, which places the English reader outside the language as the son is partly outside it.
literary_significance: The poem is a frequent anthology selection from Rose and is regularly taught in courses on diaspora poetry; with 'Persimmons' it shows the two ways Lee handles the loss of a language - by reclaiming a word and by letting the mother's song stand untranslated.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Rose (Rochester, NY: BOA Editions, 1986). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is exile and the memory of a homeland known through song rather than through experience. The second is the mother's voice as an inheritance. The third is the family as a small audience for one another. The fourth is art as the container of what cannot be said directly.
summary: The poem's situation is a room in America and a mother singing a song about lotus and water in a place she left; the father joins in, and the poem describes the song's effect on the listeners - the water rising in the room, the two of them in a boat on the lake, the grandmother in the song weeping. It ends with the singer and the listeners inside the song's landscape, and with the recognition that the song is where the country now is.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem's untranslated song as its central gesture, since the reader is not given the words and must take the song's effect on faith; the standard account of Rose places it with the poems that make the mother rather than the father the vehicle of memory.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from the collection; a first periodical appearance, if any, was not established.

title: People Like That Are the Only People Here: Canonical Babbling in Peed Onk
description: 'People Like That Are the Only People Here: Canonical Babbling in Peed Onk' appeared in The New Yorker in 1997 and was collected in Birds of America (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1998). It is a second-person story about a mother whose baby is diagnosed with cancer, written from the experience of Lorrie Moore's own son's illness.
plot_or_argument: The story's title comes from the sign on a hospital door, and the story's subject is the language of catastrophe: the parents on the ward speak in a code of proper nouns and euphemisms, the medical staff speak in another, and the writer among them is expected to translate. Moore's second person is the story's central technical decision - it puts the reader in the mother's position while also making the mother a character being observed, which allows the story to be funny about the unbearable without ever suggesting the suffering is bearable. The jokes are the story's way of keeping faith with the wards: the husband's parsimony, the other mothers' gossip, the grandmother's telephone calls about meatloaf. The ending's turn to writing - the narrator is asked to produce an account and the story becomes that account - is the story's argument about what literature can do with a sick child, which is not to cure but to bear witness and to bill someone for it. It is the most formally daring story in Birds of America and the one that made Moore's collection a critical reference point. Its title, taken from a hospital door sign and from the clinical phrase for a baby's babble, is the story's thesis: the ward has its own language, and the writer's job is to learn it without becoming fluent enough to stop noticing how strange it is.
narrative_structure: A story that moves from a third-person opening into a sustained second-person address, in episodic scenes of the ward, ending on the narrator's acknowledgement of the book she must write.
meter_and_prosody: Second-person narration; a comic voice that puns and parodies the medical and the domestic; long accumulative sentences; and a refusal of sentiment at the moments of greatest pain.
historical_context: The story appeared in The New Yorker in 1997 and in Birds of America in 1998; Moore's son was treated for a rare cancer as a small child in the mid-1990s, and she has said the story came directly from the ward. The collection won the Irish Times International Fiction Prize and belongs to the late-1990s boom in American short-story writing, when The New Yorker's fiction was again a national forum.
literary_significance: The story is one of the most discussed American short stories of the 1990s and is regularly taught as an example of the comic treatment of trauma and of second-person narration; it is the Norton's only Moore selection. Its publication in The New Yorker in 1997 placed it at the centre of the decade's literary conversation.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker in 1997; collected in Birds of America (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1998). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is childhood illness and the medical institution, treated with the exactness of a witness who has been inside it. The second is the language of catastrophe and the euphemisms that make it survivable. The third is the writer's obligation, since the story turns on being asked to write. The fourth is marriage under pressure, which the story renders through the husband's jokes and his attention to money.
summary: The story opens in the third person, with a mother finding blood in her baby's diaper, and then shifts into the second person, addressing 'you' as the mother through the diagnosis, the hospital, the ward the parents call Peed Onk (pediatric oncology) and the surgery. On the ward she meets the other parents, whose children are dying, and she becomes the one who is asked to write things down - the other mothers want her, as the writer, to record it. Her husband negotiates the bills and makes jokes; the narrator watches herself and the other parents with a comic cruelty that is also a form of love. The story ends with a demand that someone write the bill, and with the narrator realizing she is the one who must.
critical_context: Criticism reads the second person as the story's ethical instrument and debates whether its comedy is a defence against sentiment or an evasion of it; the standard account treats the story as Moore's most formally ambitious work. It is regularly discussed in medical humanities courses as a text about the language of illness, and its ending - the mother accepting that she must write the bill - is read as Moore's clearest statement about a writer's obligation to the material that has hurt her.
research_notes: The New Yorker appearance of 1997 is the date the Norton list carries; the story's text was read from the collection, which may differ from the magazine version. The title's two halves are given as the anthology gives them.

title: Domestic Work
description: Domestic Work (Saint Paul: Graywolf Press, 2000) is Natasha Trethewey's first collection, chosen by Rita Dove for the Cave Canem Poetry Prize. The Norton prints 'White Lies' and 'Vignette' from it, and the book is the earliest of the anthology's selections dated 2000.
plot_or_argument: Domestic Work is the book in which Trethewey established the method that has organised her career: the use of documents - photographs, records, advertisements, the archival photographs of Mississippi - as the starting point for a formal, controlled lyric. Its first two sections are autobiographical, and their subject is the racial order of a Southern town experienced by a child who embodies its contradiction: 'White Lies' is the poem in which that contradiction becomes a technique, since the child's lies are a way of telling the truth about a society that requires them. 'Vignette' works the other way, taking a photograph and reading the relations it records - the two girls, the car, the distance between them - without commentary, which is the method Trethewey would develop in Native Guard. The book's title names the labour of the women in the speaker's family, and the collection's interest in domestic work is also an interest in the formal work of the poem, so that the title's pun on work is deliberate. It is a first book of unusual assurance, and its publication by Graywolf under Dove's judgeship placed Trethewey at the start of a line of documentary poets that runs into the 2000s.
narrative_structure: Four sections of short formal lyrics - many in received forms or tight free verse - with the autobiographical poems first and the documentary and historical poems after; 'Vignette' is a single short poem built from a photograph.
meter_and_prosody: Tight, often rhymed or near-rhymed lines; plain diction with a strong rhythmic close; photographic and documentary material; and a first person that reports rather than confesses.
historical_context: Domestic Work appeared from Graywolf in 2000 after winning the inaugural Cave Canem Poetry Prize, judged by Rita Dove; Cave Canem, founded in 1996, was the workshop that transformed African American poetry in the late 1990s, and Trethewey's book was among its first published products. The book's Mississippi poems belong to the years of her childhood in Gulfport, and its archival poems precede Native Guard (2006).
literary_significance: Domestic Work established Trethewey as the leading documentary poet of her generation and is the book through which the Norton represents the 2000 end of the period; its two selections give the anthology the autobiographical and the archival sides of her method. The book's Cave Canem prize is a marker of the institutional transformation of African American poetry in the 1990s.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Graywolf Press (Saint Paul, Minnesota) in 2000. The Norton prints 'White Lies' and 'Vignette'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the racial order of the segregated or post-segregated South, seen from a biracial child's position. The second is the photographic archive and what it records and omits. The third is domestic labour and the women who performed it, which the title names as both the subject and the method. The fourth is history, both family and national, as the material of lyric, and running through all of them is the formal discipline that lets a photograph or a record become a poem without being explained.
summary: The book is in four sections, and its poems are about the speaker's childhood in Gulfport, Mississippi, as the daughter of a white father and a Black mother, and about the domestic workers of her family's past. 'White Lies' is a poem about a child who lies about her address, her colour and her mother to survive the racial rules of her town; 'Vignette' is a short poem built from a photograph of two girls, one white and one Black, standing together in front of a car. The collection's later sections turn to the Civil War and to the photographic record of African Americans in the nineteenth century.
critical_context: Criticism reads the collection as the beginning of Trethewey's documentary project and discusses 'White Lies' as a poem about the child's necessary duplicity; the standard account of her development treats Domestic Work as the foundation on which Native Guard built. The book's formal control is usually noted as unusual in a first collection.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the two printed poems were read in their published form and the description of the book's structure rests on its table of contents and the standard critical accounts.

title: Interpreter of Maladies
description: 'Interpreter of Maladies' appeared in The New Yorker in 1998 and gave its title to Jhumpa Lahiri's first collection (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1999), which won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2000. The Norton prints it, and it is the story through which the anthology represents the 1990s literature of the South Asian diaspora.
plot_or_argument: The story's organising figure is interpretation, and its achievement is to make the title's job do three kinds of work at once: Kapasi translates languages, he reads the Das family's marriage, and he misreads Mrs Das's interest in him. Lahiri builds the story on the gap between what is said and what is meant, and her technique is to keep the narration close to Kapasi's own misunderstanding, so that the reader sees what he does not. Mrs Das's confession - that one of her children is not her husband's - is delivered to a stranger because he is safe, and the story's cruelty is that her confidence is a transaction to her and a revelation to him. The paper with his address blowing away is the story's final image of the distance between fantasy and life, and it has become one of the most discussed endings in contemporary American short fiction. Lahiri's prose is plain, patient and exact, and its refusal of epiphany is what distinguishes her from the generation of story writers who ended on revelation. Lahiri's Indian setting is deliberately touristic: the Das family sees the Sun Temple through a guidebook and a car window, and Kapasi's own relation to the country is entirely working, which is the distance the story measures without ever formulating.
narrative_structure: A third-person narrative restricted to Kapasi's point of view, in a single continuous episode - the car, the temple, the return - with a confession at the centre and an open, unresolved ending.
literary_form: Short story (title story of the collection)
meter_and_prosody: Plain, patient third-person prose; exact sensory detail of the Indian landscape and the car; free indirect discourse for Kapasi's thoughts; and a refusal of the epiphany at the close.
historical_context: The story appeared in The New Yorker in 1998 and in Interpreter of Maladies in 1999, which won the Pulitzer in 2000; its setting is the tourist circuit from Puri to Konarak in Orissa, and its material is the annual visit of Americanised Indian families to a country their children regard as foreign. The collection belongs to the years in which South Asian American writing entered the mainstream, alongside the work of Bharati Mukherjee and Vikram Chandra.
literary_significance: The story is the most anthologised piece of South Asian American fiction of the 1990s and the title story of the collection that won the Pulitzer Prize in 2000; it is the Norton's selection from Lahiri. Its handling of the failed epiphany is regularly taught as a model of the contemporary short-story ending.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker in 1998; collected in Interpreter of Maladies (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1999). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Indian American family abroad, which Lahiri presents as neither exotic nor exemplary. The second is the marriage of Mr and Mrs Das, rendered through the gaps in their talk. The third is language and translation, both literal and figurative. The fourth is the loneliness of the immigrant wife, which the story treats with sympathy and no judgment.
summary: Mr and Mrs Das, Indian Americans from Massachusetts, are on a tour of India with their three children and their guide, Mr Kapasi, who drives them to the Sun Temple at Konarak. Kapasi works part of the week as an interpreter for a doctor, translating Gujarati patients' symptoms into English and the doctor's instructions back again. Mrs Das becomes interested in this work and tells him that she has something to interpret - an unnamed illness, and then an admission about her life. The story ends with the family driving on and Kapasi's idea of the woman collapsing into the ordinary, with a piece of paper carrying his address blowing away in the dust.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story through the figure of the interpreter and discusses Lahiri's refusal of revelation as her departure from the Joycean story; the standard account of the collection treats the Das marriage as a study of the distances inside an immigrant family. The story is regularly taught with Lahiri's later work in Italian as a pair of essays in translation.
research_notes: The New Yorker appearance of 1998 is the date the Norton list carries; the text was read from the collection, which may differ from the magazine version.

title: Drown
description: 'Drown' is the last story of Junot Díaz's first collection, Drown (New York: Riverhead Books, 1996). It is narrated by Yunior, the character who recurs through the book and through Díaz's later fiction, and it is the story in which he and his friend Beto come back together after Beto has left for college.
plot_or_argument: 'Drown' is the story in which Díaz's central subject comes into focus: the way a man's shame about his own past shapes his relation to everyone he loves. The story is almost without plot, and its method is a first-person narration that withholds until the last possible moment, so that the reader assembles the significance of Beto's visit only as Yunior himself admits it. The prose is short, blunt and full of the cadences of Dominican American English, and Díaz leaves Spanish in it without gloss, which was one of the things that made the collection new. The title's figure - drowning - runs through the story as the fear of being pulled under by the past, and the final scene in the water gives the metaphor a physical form without stating it. As the closing story of the collection, 'Drown' returns to the material of the opening stories and refuses the upward movement of the immigrant narrative: Yunior has not left, and the story's honesty about that is what made Díaz's book a departure from the success-story template of the 1990s. Díaz's decision to leave the encounter with Beto unnamed keeps the story from becoming a coming-out narrative; what matters is the shame the narrator cannot acknowledge, and the withholding is how the story makes the reader feel it.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative in short sentences, moving between the present reunion and remembered boyhood, with a withheld revelation and a final scene in the water.
literary_form: Short story (title story of the collection)
meter_and_prosody: Short, blunt sentences in a demotic New Jersey Dominican English; Spanish unglossed; a narration that withholds and then admits; and a refusal of metaphor that leaves the water literal.
historical_context: Drown appeared from Riverhead in 1996, the year of the Dominican American community's emergence as a literary subject, and its stories had appeared in magazines through the early 1990s; its Spanish, its drugs and its refusal of uplift distinguished it from the immigrant novels of the 1980s. The same narrator and family appear in The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao (2007) and This Is How You Lose Her (2012), so that 'Drown' is now read as the beginning of a multi-volume fictional world.
literary_significance: The story is the title piece of the collection that made Díaz a central figure of 1990s American fiction and a standard text of the Latino and immigrant canon; it is the Norton's selection from Drown, and it is regularly taught as an example of the refusal of the immigrant success narrative. Its narrator's later importance makes it the founding story of Díaz's fictional world.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Drown (New York: Riverhead Books, 1996). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the friendship between two boys and the shame that has grown into it. The second is sexuality and the unspoken, since the story's central fact is implied rather than stated. The third is the Dominican diaspora in New Jersey, its work and its drug economy. The fourth is the refusal of the immigrant success narrative, which the collection's ending deliberately withholds.
summary: Yunior is in his early twenties, living in New Jersey, doing factory work and selling drugs, and Beto has returned from college for a visit. The two of them were close as boys, and the story's present is their reunion: they smoke, they talk, they go to the beach, and Beto tells Yunior about the life he has left them both for. Yunior's narration keeps the friendship's history - the two of them as boys, the shame of Yunior's family, the implication of a sexual encounter years earlier that Yunior has never acknowledged - just off the surface of the story, and the ending leaves Yunior alone in the water.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story through its withheld revelation and its refusal of closure, and discusses Díaz's code-switching as a political as well as a stylistic choice; the standard account of Drown treats the title story as its most formally controlled piece. The 2018 allegations against Díaz are part of the reception history and are not part of the story's analysis.
research_notes: The collection's 1996 date is confirmed from its imprint; the story's first periodical appearance, if any, was not established for this record.

title: Adolescence
description: 'Adolescence' is a sequence of three numbered poems that the Norton Anthology of American Literature prints as three separate selections dated 1980.
