The sequence belongs to Rita Dove's early work with the Akron material of her first two books, and it is read here as one work because the three poems are numbered parts of a single sequence.
plot_or_argument: The sequence's subject is the acquisition of a woman's knowledge, and its method is the withholding of the adult's judgement. Dove writes the girl's experience without either nostalgia or indictment, and the effect is of a world observed from inside a consciousness that is only beginning to understand what is being done to it. The numbering matters: the three poems are stages rather than episodes, and the sequence's refusal to resolve makes it one of the more formally interesting pieces of Dove's early work. The poems' plain diction and short lines are close to the Akron poems of Thomas and Beulah, which were written a few years later, and the sequence can be read as the workshop in which Dove developed the voice she would give her grandmother.
narrative_structure: Three numbered short lyrics forming a single sequence, moving from the body to the social world and ending without resolution.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines and plain diction; a third person that moves close to the girl's consciousness; an absence of the adult's commentary; and images drawn from household and small-town life.
historical_context: The sequence belongs to Dove's early Akron material and to the years between her first two collections; the Norton dates it 1980, the year of The Yellow House on the Corner, and treats its three parts as separate selections. The poems' subject, a Black girl's adolescence in small-town Ohio, is the same ground as Thomas and Beulah's later sequence.
literary_significance: The sequence is a Norton selection in three parts and represents the early Dove in the anthology alongside 'Geometry' and 'Parsley'; it is the only place in the anthology where a single sequence is printed as three separate items, which is why this record identifies the three rows as one work.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E, as three numbered poems dated 1980. The first printing of the sequence as a whole was not established for this record.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is adolescence and the body's education. The second is gender, since the poems record the different rules a girl learns. The third is the family and its silences. The fourth is the town and the small society that watches the girl.
summary: The three poems follow a girl through the physical and social education of adolescence in small-town Ohio: the body changing, the attention of boys and men, the rules of a household, and the gap between what is happening and what can be said about it. Each poem is a short lyric in the third person or a lightly marked first person, and the sequence moves by association rather than by narrative, so that the three poems together form a portrait rather than a story.
critical_context: Criticism treats the early Dove poems about adolescence as the foundation of her later narrative sequences and reads the withholding of judgement as characteristic of her manner; the sequence has attracted less individual commentary than 'Parsley' or Thomas and Beulah.
research_notes: The three poems were read in the form the anthology prints them; their first book appearance was not verified, and the record therefore dates them as the Norton list does, 1980, rather than assigning a collection. This is the only record in the installment that answers three anthology rows.

title: Parsley
description: 'Parsley' is in Museum (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1983), Rita Dove's second collection. It is a four-part poem about the 1937 massacre of Haitian cane-cutters in the Dominican Republic on the orders of Rafael Trujillo, and it is built on the shibboleth 'perejil', the Spanish word for parsley, which Trujillo's soldiers used to identify Haitians by their accent.
plot_or_argument: 'Parsley' is the most ambitious poem in Museum and one of the most important American poems of the 1980s. Its achievement is to make a linguistic fact - the inability to pronounce a word correctly - into the form as well as the subject of the poem, so that repetition, which is normally a device of lyric incantation, becomes an instrument of murder. The general's voice is the poem's boldest decision: Dove gives Trujillo a self-justifying aria, and the effect is not to humanise him but to show the banality of the reasoning that produced the massacre. The chorus of cane-cutters is the poem's ethical centre, and Dove gives them the dignity of a collective voice rather than individual suffering. The poem's structure - four numbered parts, moving between the killers and the killed - is operatic, and its scale is unusual in an American lyric of the period. It has been criticised for speaking for Haitian victims from outside their experience, and defended on the grounds that its subject is precisely the way a language can be made into a border. The poem's research was drawn from accounts of the massacre, and its historical accuracy about the shibboleth is the foundation of its argument. The general's monologue is also a study in self-pity: he complains that he has been misunderstood, and the poem lets his grievance stand beside the bodies without comment.
narrative_structure: Four numbered parts: a chorus of cane-cutters, the general's monologue, a sequence of massacre images, and the general's return; the whole built on the repetition of a single word across the parts.
meter_and_prosody: Repetition of 'perejil' as a structural device; multiple voices in a single poem; plain declarative lines for the historical passages; and a musical, almost liturgical movement between the parts.
historical_context: Museum appeared in 1983, after Dove's Fulbright year in Germany, and 'Parsley' was researched from the historical record of the 1937 massacre, in which Trujillo's soldiers killed between seventeen and twenty thousand Haitians living in the Dominican borderlands. The poem's attention to the shibboleth comes from the accounts of survivors, and its publication in 1983 preceded by two decades the fuller historiography of the massacre in English.
literary_significance: 'Parsley' is the poem for which Dove was first widely recognised and remains one of the most anthologised American poems about state violence; its four-part form and its use of multiple voices have been widely imitated. It is a Norton selection, and with Thomas and Beulah it makes Dove the best-represented poet in the anthology's period.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Museum (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1983). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the 1937 massacre and the racial logic that produced it. The second is language as a border and as an instrument of violence. The third is the banality of the perpetrator's reasoning, which the poem gives voice to rather than reports. The fourth is the possibility of representing atrocity at all, which the poem's formal ambition raises directly.
summary: The poem's first part is a chorus of the cane-cutters, who repeat the word 'perejil' and wait for the general; the second is the general's own voice, and the third is a sequence of images from the massacre; the fourth returns to the general, who cannot pronounce the word himself, and to the silence afterwards. The poem's language circles the single word, and its repetitions become the mechanism of the killing: the failure to trill the 'r' is the death sentence, and the poem makes the reader hear it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a landmark of the American historical lyric and debates the ethics of Dove's multiple voicing; the standard account treats the shibboleth as the poem's formal principle as well as its subject. It is regularly taught with Maus and with the poetry of the Holocaust as an example of the representation of atrocity.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from its published text; the casualty figures are given as the historical estimates give them, not as the poem states them, and the poem does not itself give a number.
